arXiv:2608.17613v1 [cs.IR] 18 Aug 2026

Once Generated, Ranked: End-to-End Generative Slate Recommendation with Unified Semantic-Collaborative IDs

Yang Hu    Jiayi Guo    Jingui Ma    Ning Li\corresponding    Jiangling Qin    Yanming Li    Yang Deng    Xiaoshuang Chen\corresponding    Kaiqiao Zhan
Abstract

Slate Recommendation treats a slate rather than an individual item as the fundamental recommendation unit, requiring list-wise optimization of item interactions and overall slate utility. However, existing approaches rely on cascaded pipelines that separate candidate generation from ranking and constrain optimization within retrieved candidates. Recently, Generative Recommendation based on Semantic ID (SID) has provided a promising direction toward end-to-end recommendation. However, existing SID construction methods often lack recommendation-aware semantics and effective integration of local collaborative signals, while current generative recommenders optimize with next-token prediction objectives that are misaligned with slate-level optimization and overall utility. To address these challenges, we propose OGR, an end-to-end generative slate recommendation framework that directly generates ordered slates without separating generation and ranking—“Once Generated, Ranked.” First, we introduce TUSID, a recommendation-aware SID construction framework that adaptively integrates item-specific semantic information and local collaborative signals to construct hierarchical SIDs for generative slate recommendation. Based on these SIDs, OGR performs list-wise preference planning to model global slate preferences and inter-item dependencies, enabling pipelined position-wise SID decoding to directly generate ordered slates. Furthermore, we propose SPA, which leverages reward-guided conservative policy optimization to align generated slates with user preferences beyond likelihood imitation. Extensive offline experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of OGR over representative baselines (+48.2%/+27.2% relative gains in NDCG@5 on industrial/public datasets), while online A/B testing on Kuaishou, a large-scale short-video platform, further confirms its practical value, yielding a 1.120% improvement in Effective Views.

Introduction

Slate Recommendation treats a slate rather than an individual item as the fundamental recommendation unit, requiring joint modeling of item interactions and optimization of list-wise objectives. Existing approaches typically follow a cascaded paradigm of candidate generation–ranking–reranking, where candidate pools are constructed through multi-stage retrieval and filtering. Although efficient for practical deployment, its optimization scope is constrained by the candidate space, making it impossible to recover potentially relevant items that are not retrieved. Moreover, the objective misalignment across different stages of the cascaded pipeline prevents end-to-end optimization, leaving candidate generation and final ranking as separated processes—“Generated, Then Ranked.”

Recently, Generative Recommendation (GR) (Rajput et al. 2023; Charikar et al. 2002) based on SID has emerged as a promising direction to overcome the limitations of candidate-constrained recommendation. By mapping items into discrete SID spaces, generative recommenders can directly generate target items from user histories, enabling an end-to-end recommendation paradigm. However, existing SID construction methods mainly focus on semantic discretization and inject collaborative information through representation alignment or contrastive regularization (Luo et al. 2025; Wang et al. 2024a; Chen et al. 2026), but do not explicitly encode distance-weighted local co-occurrence distributions for slate construction. Moreover, existing GR methods usually optimize autoregressive SID generation with the Next Token Prediction (NTP) objective, which is inherently misaligned with the list-wise optimization of overall slate utility. Additionally, such token-level likelihood optimization focuses on predicting individual SID tokens rather than capturing user preference over the entire slate, limiting the potential of GR in Slate Recommendation.

To address these challenges, we first propose Two-stage Unified SID Construction (TUSID), tailored to generative slate recommendation. TUSID extracts rich item information from multimodal semantics and structured high-level attributes, and performs recommendation-aware adaptive fusion to obtain semantic representations that are customized to different items and recommendation scenarios. Furthermore, we introduce a CountSketch-based collaborative injection mechanism to incorporate local user behavioral co-occurrence structures, together with confidence-aware fusion to regulate the contribution of collaborative signals. The resulting unified representations are quantized by residual K-means (RQ-KMeans) (Charikar et al. 2002) into recommendation-aware hierarchical SIDs.

Based on the proposed SID, we further introduce OGR, an end-to-end generative slate recommendation framework. Different from existing generative methods that focus on next-item generation, OGR uses a listwise preference planner to capture the global slate structure and dependencies across display positions. Once the planned preference representation for a position becomes available, its SID chain is decoded while the planner proceeds to subsequent positions, forming a pipeline that avoids serial item-by-item SID generation. We further introduce Slate-Level Preference Alignment (SPA), which derives calibrated preference signals from user-feedback-based primary rewards and slate-level auxiliary rewards. Conservative policy optimization then aligns generated slates beyond likelihood imitation while preventing excessive deviation from the reference policy. Together, OGR unifies item-level generation and listwise organization—“Once Generated, Ranked.”

Extensive experiments on both large-scale industrial data and public benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of OGR, while online A/B testing on Kuaishou, a real-world recommendation platform serving hundreds of millions of daily active users, further confirms its practical value.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose TUSID, a recommendation-aware SID construction framework that adaptively integrates item-specific semantic information and local collaborative signals to construct hierarchical SIDs for generative slate recommendation.

  • •

    We propose OGR, an end-to-end generative slate recommendation framework that combines list-wise preference planning with pipelined position-wise SID decoding. We further introduce SPA to align generated slates with user preferences through calibrated multi-objective rewards and conservative policy optimization. We further introduce SPA to align generated slates with user preferences through calibrated multi-objective rewards and conservative policy optimization.

  • •

    Extensive offline experiments on industrial and public datasets, together with online A/B testing results, demonstrate the effectiveness and practical impact of our methods.

Related Works

Slate Recommendation jointly selects and orders multiple items by modeling inter-item interactions and listwise utility. However, existing methods (Pei et al. 2019; Bello et al. 2018; Fu et al. 2026; Xu et al. 2023; Pang et al. 2026) are typically formulated over retrieved candidate sets or predefined action spaces, leaving slate quality bounded by upstream selection. Pioneered by TIGER (Rajput et al. 2023), SID-based GR enables end-to-end recommendation by generating hierarchical semantic identifiers instead of atomic item IDs in conventional sequential recommenders (Xie et al. 2022; Qiu et al. 2022; Rendle et al. 2009; Du et al. 2023; Sarwar et al. 2001; Yue et al. 2024). Subsequent studies extend this paradigm through recommendation-aware SID construction with semantic–collaborative alignment (Zheng et al. 2024; Wang et al. 2024a; Pan et al. 2026; Hidasi et al. 2016; Li et al. 2025; Xiao et al. 2026), joint SID–recommendation optimization (Liu et al. 2024; Kabbur et al. 2013), and efficient generation through tree-structured or hybrid retrieval, order-agnostic and parallel generation, and decoding/cache acceleration (Si et al. 2024; Hu et al. 2026; Hou et al. 2025; Qu et al. 2025; Lin et al. 2025a; Lin et al. 2025b; Yang et al. 2025a). However, prevailing NTP objectives optimize the likelihood of individual SID tokens rather than inter-item dependencies and overall slate utility, limiting the effectiveness of the generative paradigm for Slate Recommendation.

Methodology

As illustrated in Figure 1, we propose OGR, an end-to-end generative slate recommendation framework that directly generates ordered slates conditioned on user histories, comprising TUSID for recommendation-aware SID construction, GL2P for list-wise slate generation, and SPA for preference alignment.

Problem Formulation

For a user uu, let ℋu=(i1,…,iT)\mathcal{H}_{u}=(i_{1},\ldots,i_{T}) denote the chronological interaction history, where iti_{t} denotes the item at the tt-th interaction. Each item ii is represented by a hierarchical DD-level SID 𝐬i=(si1,…,siD)\mathbf{s}_{i}=(s_{i}^{1},\ldots,s_{i}^{D}). Given ℋu\mathcal{H}_{u}, OGR parameterized by θ\theta directly generates an ordered SID slate 𝒮^u\widehat{\mathcal{S}}_{u} of size KK and maps it into an item slate:

𝒮^u=Fθ​(ℋu),𝒴^u=Map⁡(𝒮^u),\widehat{\mathcal{S}}_{u}=F_{\theta}(\mathcal{H}_{u}),\qquad\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{u}=\mathrm{Map}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}_{u}), (1)

where Map⁡(⋅)\mathrm{Map}(\cdot) denotes SID-to-item lookup. Training uses the observed exposure slate 𝒴u=(y1,…,yK)\mathcal{Y}_{u}=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{K}) and associated feedback signals 𝒲u=(w1,…,wK)\mathcal{W}_{u}=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{K}), where yky_{k} and wkw_{k} denote the item and its feedback at slate position kk, respectively.

Two-Stage Unified SID Construction (TUSID)

To construct SIDs tailored to generative slate recommendation, we propose TUSID, as illustrated in Figure 2.

Semantic Fusion

Existing SID methods mainly rely on general content representations, which may underrepresent structured high-level attributes whose relevance varies across items in recommendation scenarios. For example, products may rely more on brand-related attributes, whereas explainer videos may benefit more from style- or audience-related attributes. To obtain item-specific semantic representations, we encode each item from two complementary views. An MLLM encodes the image, audio, and text of item ii into a fine-grained semantic representation eiMe_{i}^{\mathrm{M}}, while a shared text encoder produces four high-level attribute representations eiae_{i}^{a}, where a∈{b,c,Bt,Ct}{\mathrm{a}}\in\{\mathrm{b},\mathrm{c},\mathrm{Bt},\mathrm{Ct}\} denotes Brand, Category, B-tags (supply-side content characteristics), and C-tags (demand-side user value), respectively. The complete attribute taxonomy is provided in the appendix.

Since different items may rely on different high-level attributes, we retain the MLLM representation as the semantic backbone and use it to adaptively aggregate item-specific attribute information. Specifically, eiMe_{i}^{\mathrm{M}} serves as the query QiQ_{i}, while ℰiattr=[eib,eic,eiBt,eiCt]⊤\mathcal{E}_{i}^{\mathrm{attr}}=[e_{i}^{\mathrm{b}},e_{i}^{\mathrm{c}},e_{i}^{\mathrm{Bt}},e_{i}^{\mathrm{Ct}}]^{\top} provides the keys KiK_{i} and values ViV_{i}. The aggregated attribute representation is computed as

hiattr=CrossAttention(Qi=eiM,Ki=Vi=ℰiattr).h_{i}^{\mathrm{attr}}=\operatorname{CrossAttention}\left(Q_{i}=e_{i}^{\mathrm{M}},K_{i}=V_{i}=\mathcal{E}_{i}^{\mathrm{attr}}\right). (2)

To regulate the overall attribute contribution, we predict a scalar sigmoid gate gig_{i} from [eiM;hiattr][e_{i}^{\mathrm{M}};h_{i}^{\mathrm{attr}}] and perform gated residual fusion:

eisem=eiM+gi​hiattr.e_{i}^{\mathrm{sem}}=e_{i}^{\mathrm{M}}+g_{i}h_{i}^{\mathrm{attr}}. (3)

This asymmetric fusion preserves the MLLM representation as the semantic backbone while introducing item-adaptive attribute residuals.

To make the fused representations recommendation-aware, we use eiseme_{i}^{\mathrm{sem}} as the item embeddings in SASRec (Kang and McAuley 2018a) and train the fusion parameters with its next-item prediction loss ℒrec\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}. We further regularize the attribute residual to prevent attribute branch from overwhelming the MLLM backbone:

ℒfusion=ℒrec+βres|ℬ|​∑i∈ℬ‖gi​hiattr‖22,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fusion}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}+\frac{\beta_{\mathrm{res}}}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}}\left\|g_{i}h_{i}^{\mathrm{attr}}\right\|_{2}^{2},\\ (4)

where ℒfusion\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fusion}} denotes the overall fusion objective, ℬ\mathcal{B} denotes the set of positive and sampled negative items in SASRec, and βres\beta_{\mathrm{res}} controls the residual regularization strength.

Collaborative Injection

Although Semantic Fusion aligns semantic representations with recommendation objectives through ℒrec\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}, it fails to capture local item-item co-occurrence structures. We instead inject collaborative information before quantization, treating collaboration as an evidence-weighted complement, allowing items with sufficient behavioral evidence to exploit collaborative structures while preserving original semantic information for sparse and cold-start items.

CountSketch-Based Collaborative Embedding (CCE).

For each user uu, we construct co-occurrences only from the high-quality positive-feedback training prefix, excluding validation and test interactions to prevent information leakage. For a center item ii at position pp, each item jj at position qq satisfying 0<|p−q|≤ω0<|p-q|\leq\omega is treated as a contextual item and assigned the distance-based weight 1/|p−q|1/|p-q| since nearby interactions may indicate stronger local interest correlations.

To avoid storing the full item-item co-occurrence matrix, we employ Signed CountSketch (Charikar et al. 2004) to compress the local contextual distribution of each item into a fixed-dimensional statistical vector. For a center item ii and its contextual item jj, the update process is defined as:

𝒞i​[h⁡(j)]←𝒞i​[h⁡(j)]+σ⁡(j)|p−q|,\mathcal{C}_{i}[h(j)]\leftarrow\mathcal{C}_{i}[h(j)]+\frac{\sigma(j)}{|p-q|}, (5)

where 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} is the collaborative sketch of item ii, h⁡(j)h(j) maps contextual item jj to a sketch coordinate, and σ⁡(j)∈{−1,+1}\sigma(j)\in\{-1,+1\} is its sign hash. Because h⁡(⋅)h(\cdot) and σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) are shared across sketches, a common contextual item contributes positively to their inner product, whereas cross terms caused by unrelated collisions have zero expectation under the random sign hash.

We further apply signed-log transformation to reduce the dominance of frequent co-occurrences, followed by normalization and random projection to obtain the dense collaborative embedding eicole_{i}^{\mathrm{col}} with the same dimensionality as eiseme_{i}^{\mathrm{sem}}.

Confidence-Aware Weighting (CAW).

During CountSketch construction, we record UiU_{i}, the number of distinct users contributing valid contextual updates to item ii, as a measure of behavioral support while limiting the influence of repeated interactions from highly active users.

Based on UiU_{i}, we define the collaborative confidence γi\gamma_{i} and fusion weight αi\alpha_{i} as:

γi=log⁡(1+Ui)log⁡(1+Ui)+τ,αi=αcol​γi,\gamma_{i}=\frac{\log(1+U_{i})}{\log(1+U_{i})+\tau},\qquad\alpha_{i}=\alpha_{\mathrm{col}}\gamma_{i}, (6)

where τ>0\tau>0 controls the saturation speed of the confidence and αcol∈[0,1]\alpha_{\mathrm{col}}\in[0,1] is the maximum collaborative weight.

A larger UiU_{i} increases the contribution of collaborative information, whereas a smaller UiU_{i} downweights unreliable behavioral evidence for interaction-sparse or cold-start items, and when Ui=γi=αi=0U_{i}=\gamma_{i}=\alpha_{i}=0, the representation relies entirely on the semantic branch, consistent with the common industrial cold-start practice of using content information to compensate for sparse behavioral evidence.

After ℓ2\ell_{2} normalization, we construct eiunie_{i}^{\mathrm{uni}} by confidence-weighted concatenation:

eiuni=[1−αi​eisem;αi​eicol].e_{i}^{\mathrm{uni}}=\left[\sqrt{1-\alpha_{i}}e_{i}^{\mathrm{sem}};\sqrt{\alpha_{i}}e_{i}^{\mathrm{col}}\right]. (7)

The square-root coefficients preserve its norm, after which RQ-KMeans quantizes eiunie_{i}^{\mathrm{uni}} into the final SIDs.

Global Listwise Preference Planning Architecture (GL2P)

Existing GR methods usually optimize autoregressive SID generation with NTP loss, which is misaligned with the slate-level optimization of item selection and ordering, limiting the explicit modeling of global slate-level preferences and inter-item dependencies. Different from next-item generation, OGR treats the entire slate as the fundamental prediction unit by combining listwise preference planning with pipelined position-wise SID decoding.

History Encoder

The history encoder Enchist\mathrm{Enc}_{\mathrm{hist}} converts the ordered SID interaction history into contextual representations by aggregating hierarchical SID embeddings and incorporating temporal information:

𝒵h\displaystyle\mathcal{Z}^{\mathrm{h}} =Enchist​([∑d=1Dℰ⁡[std]+pth]t=1T),\displaystyle=\mathrm{Enc}_{\mathrm{hist}}\left([\sum_{d=1}^{D}\mathcal{E}[s_{t}^{d}]+p^{\mathrm{h}}_{t}]_{t=1}^{T}\right), (8)

where ℰ\mathcal{E} denotes the shared SID embedding table and pthp^{\mathrm{h}}_{t} denotes the temporal embedding at position tt.

List-Wise Preference Planner

Rather than directly decoding item SIDs, OGR models cross-item dependencies in a coarse-grained preference space through the preference planner. During training, the planner adopts teacher forcing. For each target item at position mm, we aggregate its DD-level SID embeddings and construct the right-shifted planner input as:

gm=∑d=1Dℰ⁡[smd],𝒬tr=[BOS,g1,…,gK−1],g_{m}=\sum_{d=1}^{D}\mathcal{E}[s_{m}^{d}],\qquad\mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm{tr}}=[\mathrm{BOS},g_{1},\ldots,g_{K-1}], (9)

where ℰ\mathcal{E} denotes the shared SID embedding table. A causally masked Transformer decoder then produces one planned preference representation for each slate position:

𝒫=Decplan⁡(𝒬tr,𝒵h)=[p1,…,pK].\mathcal{P}=\operatorname{Dec}_{\mathrm{plan}}(\mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm{tr}},\mathcal{Z}^{\mathrm{h}})=[p_{1},\ldots,p_{K}]. (10)

Causal self-attention captures dependencies among preceding slate positions, while cross-attention retrieves signals relevant to the user’s preferences from 𝒵h\mathcal{Z}^{\mathrm{h}}. During inference, the planner starts from BOS\mathrm{BOS} and autoregressively feeds the previously generated representation pm−1p_{m-1} to produce pmp_{m}. Once pmp_{m} becomes available, the decoder starts generating the SID chain at position mm while the planner proceeds to position m+1m+1, forming a pipeline between preference planning and SID decoding.

Position-Wise SID Decoder

For the mm-th position, SID tokens are generated autoregressively conditioned on the planned preference embedding pmp_{m}, preceding SID tokens sm<ds_{m}^{<d}, and historical representations 𝒵h\mathcal{Z}^{\mathrm{h}}:

𝐬m=Decsid​(pm,ℰ⁡[sm<d],𝒵h).\mathbf{s}_{m}=\mathrm{Dec}_{\mathrm{sid}}\left(p_{m},\mathcal{E}[s_{m}^{<d}],\mathcal{Z}^{\mathrm{h}}\right). (11)

Since cross-position dependencies are captured by the listwise preference planner, the SID chain at each position can be decoded independently once its planned representation pmp_{m} becomes available. This allows current-position SID decoding to overlap with subsequent preference planning, yielding pipelined execution while preserving intra-item SID dependencies.

Feedback-Aware Supervision

We construct two complementary supervision sequences over the same target slate: the exposure sequence 𝒴ueps\mathcal{Y}^{\mathrm{eps}}_{u} maintains the original display order, whereas the feedback sequence 𝒴ufb\mathcal{Y}^{\mathrm{fb}}_{u} rearranges items according to their observed item-level feedback. For each supervision type o∈{eps,fb}o\in\{\mathrm{eps},\mathrm{fb}\}, the SID generation loss is defined as:

ℒsido=−1|𝒰|​K​D∑u∑m=1K∑d=1Dlogπu,mo,d[su,mo,d],\mathcal{L}^{o}_{\mathrm{sid}}=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{U}|KD}\sum_{u}\sum_{m=1}^{K}\sum_{d=1}^{D}\log\pi^{o,d}_{u,m}[s^{o,d}_{u,m}], (12)

where su,mo,ds^{o,d}_{u,m} denotes the target SID token at depth dd, πu,mo,d​[su,mo,d]\pi^{o,d}_{u,m}[s^{o,d}_{u,m}] denotes its predicted probability, and |𝒰||\mathcal{U}| denotes the number of training users.

Thus, the supervised training objective is:

ℒsup=ℒsideps+α​ℒsidfb,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sup}}=\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{eps}}_{\mathrm{sid}}+\alpha\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{fb}}_{\mathrm{sid}}, (13)

where α\alpha controls the strength of feedback-aware supervision.

Under this supervision scheme, the exposure branch preserves fidelity to logged slate distributions, while the feedback branch injects user preference signals into the generation process.

Slate-Level Preference Alignment (SPA)

Although feedback-aware supervised learning provides OGR with both exposure-order and feedback-informed supervision, it remains a likelihood-based imitation of fixed targets and lacks the ability to optimize relative preferences among multiple generated slates. Inspired by preference alignment methods in large language models (Rafailov et al. 2023; Koren et al. 2009), we propose a preference alignment post-training stage to further align generated slates with user preferences.

Candidate Rollouts

Let θ0\theta_{0} denote the frozen supervised model as the reference policy. For each user uu, we perform beam search at each slate position using its corresponding planned preference embedding and combine the generated candidates into a non-duplicate slate-level action set 𝒜u\mathcal{A}_{u}. Each action a∈𝒜ua\in\mathcal{A}_{u} is defined as:

a=(𝐬u,1,…,𝐬u,K),a=(\mathbf{s}_{u,1},\ldots,\mathbf{s}_{u,K}),

where 𝐬u,k\mathbf{s}_{u,k} denotes the SID sequence at position kk and the reference log-likelihood of a candidate slate is computed as:

ℓ0​(a|u)=∑m=1K∑d=1Dlog⁡pθ0​(su,md∣𝒵uh,pu,m,su,m<d),\ell_{0}(a|u)=\sum_{m=1}^{K}\sum_{d=1}^{D}\log p_{\theta_{0}}\left(s^{d}_{u,m}\mid\mathcal{Z}^{\mathrm{h}}_{u},p_{u,m},s^{<d}_{u,m}\right), (14)

where pu,mp_{u,m} denotes the position-aware preference embedding generated by the List-Wise Preference Planner.

Reward-Consistent Calibration

To evaluate candidate slates from multiple perspectives, we define a primary reward rprir_{\mathrm{pri}} that measures slate-level user preference by aggregating feedback signals over the entire slate, such as effective views and likes, and an auxiliary reward rauxr_{\mathrm{aux}} that provides additional guidance through slate-level quality signals, such as diversity. The details are provided in the appendix.

For o∈{pri,aux}o\in\{\mathrm{pri},\mathrm{aux}\}, we standardize rewards within 𝒜u\mathcal{A}_{u} to obtain the relative reward score δu,ao\delta^{o}_{u,a}, and the final calibrated preference signal Δu,a\Delta_{u,a} is computed as:

κu,a\displaystyle\kappa_{u,a} ={min⁡(|δu,apri|,|δu,aaux|)max⁡(|δu,apri|,|δu,aaux|,ε),δu,apri⋅δu,aaux>0,0,otherwise,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\min\big(|\delta^{\mathrm{pri}}_{u,a}|,|\delta^{\mathrm{aux}}_{u,a}|\big)}{\max\big(|\delta^{\mathrm{pri}}_{u,a}|,|\delta^{\mathrm{aux}}_{u,a}|,\varepsilon\big)},&\delta^{\mathrm{pri}}_{u,a}\cdot\delta^{\mathrm{aux}}_{u,a}>0,\\[8.0pt] 0,&\mathrm{otherwise},\end{cases} (15)
Δu,a\displaystyle\Delta_{u,a} =δu,apri+κu,a​δu,aaux.\displaystyle=\delta^{\mathrm{pri}}_{u,a}+\kappa_{u,a}\delta^{\mathrm{aux}}_{u,a}.

Here, κu,a\kappa_{u,a} scales the auxiliary contribution according to the relative score magnitudes and suppresses it when the primary and auxiliary scores have conflicting directions, and ε>0\varepsilon>0 avoids division by zero. Consequently, the calibration preserves the primary recommendation objective while incorporating reliable auxiliary signals, resulting in a more robust preference alignment process.

Conservative Policy Optimization

Given the same candidate action sets, we compute the importance ratio ρu,a=exp⁡(ℓθ​(a∣u)−ℓ0​(a∣u))\rho_{u,a}=\exp(\ell_{\theta}(a\mid u)-\ell_{0}(a\mid u)) and optimize the clipped policy objective (Schulman et al. 2017):

ℒpol\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pol}} =−1NA∑u∑a∈𝒜umin{ρu,aΔu,a,\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{N_{A}}\sum_{u}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{u}}\min\Bigl\{\rho_{u,a}\Delta_{u,a}, (16)
clip(ρu,a,1−ϵ,1+ϵ)Δu,a}.\displaystyle\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\rho_{u,a},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon\right)\Delta_{u,a}\Bigr\}.

where NAN_{A} denotes the number of retained user-action pairs and ϵ\epsilon is the clipping radius.

To further constrain policy drift, we derive the candidate slate distributions from the reference and current policy likelihoods: q0​(a∣u)=softmaxa∈𝒜u​(ℓ0​(a∣u))q_{0}(a\mid u)=\mathrm{softmax}_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{u}}(\ell_{0}(a\mid u)) and qθ​(a∣u)=softmaxa∈𝒜u​(ℓθ​(a∣u))q_{\theta}(a\mid u)=\mathrm{softmax}_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{u}}(\ell_{\theta}(a\mid u)) . Their divergence is then defined as:

ℒKL=1NU​∑u∑a∈𝒜uq0​(a∣u)​log⁡q0​(a∣u)qθ​(a∣u),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}=\frac{1}{N_{U}}\sum_{u}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{u}}q_{0}(a\mid u)\log\frac{q_{0}(a\mid u)}{q_{\theta}(a\mid u)}, (17)

where NUN_{U} denotes the number of retained users. We additionally replay the supervised objective ℒsup\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sup}} and the final alignment objective is as follows:

ℒSPA=ℒpol+γ​ℒKL+η​ℒsup.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPA}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pol}}+\gamma\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}+\eta\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sup}}. (18)

where γ\gamma and η\eta denote the corresponding weights.

During refinement, we update only the List-Wise Preference Planner and the Position-Wise SID Decoder, while keeping remaining model components frozen. Consequently, slate-level planning and item-level decoding are jointly aligned with user feedback while avoiding excessive deviation from the supervised generation policy.

Experiment

Experimental Settings

Datasets and Evaluation Metrics

We conduct experiments on KuaiRec (Gao et al. 2022) and a proprietary industrial dataset collected from Kuaishou. The industrial dataset contains interaction sequences, multimodal content, high-level attributes, exposure logs, and item-level feedback. For both datasets, interactions are chronologically ordered and evaluated using a leave-five-out protocol. We report Hit Rate, Recall, and NDCG (Järvelin and Kekäläinen 2002) on positive-feedback lists to assess the model’s ability to capture users’ preference, and additionally report impression-based Hit Rate and Recall on logged exposures to evaluate the model’s ability to capture observed exposure patterns.

Implementation Details

All offline experiments are conducted on NVIDIA L20 GPUs. We use a maximum history length of 128 and generate slates of size 5. The SID tokenizer adopts a four-level configuration with a codebook size of 1,024 at each level. During inference, we perform beam search with a beam width of 20. Additional implementation details are provided in the appendix.

Results

Overall Performance Comparison

As shown in Table 1, we compare OGR against three categories of baselines: sequential recommenders (Caser, SASRec, and BERT4Rec) (Tang and Wang 2018b; Kang and McAuley 2018a; Sun et al. 2019), listwise rerankers (PRM and Seq2Slate) (Pei et al. 2019; Bello et al. 2018), and generative recommenders (TIGER and OneRec) (Rajput et al. 2023; Charikar et al. 2002). All generative baselines are implemented with comparable parameter sizes to OGR (32 MB).

Discriminative sequential recommendation methods directly estimate item scores and select the highest-scoring items, leading to stable performance in Top-5 recommendation. Listwise reranking methods explicitly model interactions among items within a candidate set and therefore provide stronger slate-level ordering ability. Meanwhile, although OneRec achieves strong Hit Rate and Recall, the method yields lower NDCG than listwise reranking baselines, highlighting a decoding dilemma: autoregressive slate generation captures cross-item dependencies but suffers from serial latency and error accumulation, whereas probability-based Top-5 selection is efficient but not listwise-aligned under NTP loss. In contrast, OGR addresses this dilemma by combining global slate planning with pipelined position-wise SID decoding, preserving cross-position dependencies while avoiding serial item-by-item SID generation and thereby achieving consistent gains across all evaluation metrics.

Comparison of SID Construction Methods

Table 2 compares SID methods (Rajput et al. 2023; Charikar et al. 2002; Wan et al. 2026; Wang et al. 2025; Zheng et al. 2024; Wang et al. 2024a) under the same OGR backbone and codebook size.

TUSID consistently outperforms all public baselines on both downstream recommendation metrics, which indicates that the resulting SIDs more effectively capture user preferences and collaborative structures. ICR and CUR measure SID uniqueness and codebook coverage (Chen et al. 2026), while Min. PPL and Top-1 Load evaluate code assignment balance by reflecting code utilization and concentration in dominant codes (Deng et al. 2025). The results show that TUSID produces collision-free SIDs while maintaining balanced code assignments across the hierarchical levels. For semantic preservation, TUSID maintains comparable V-measure (Rosenberg and Hirschberg 2007) and SC (Wan et al. 2026), which evaluate category consistency and semantic cohesion, respectively. This result suggests that effective SIDs require a balance of semantic preservation, collaborative structure, and codebook quality rather than optimizing a single metric.

Ablation Study of SID Construction

Table 3 further investigates the contribution of each component in TUSID. Compared with cross-attention and gated fusion, direct addition of high-level attributes yields lower performance, indicating that naive fusion of heterogeneous semantic sources can disrupt the original semantic structure. For collaborative injection, CCE with concatenation outperforms both additive fusion and InfoNCE-based collaborative supervision, showing that preserving complementary semantic and collaborative structures is more effective than collapsing them into a shared space. CAW further improves performance, demonstrating that confidence-based scaling of collaborative information helps prevent sparse or accidental interactions from being amplified into reliable preference signals.

Ablation Study of Slate Generation and Alignment

Table 4 evaluates the major components of GL2P and SPA. Removing the List-Wise Planner substantially degrades both metrics despite reallocating its parameter budget to the Encoder/Decoder, demonstrating that global preference planning is essential for coordinating item selection and slate ordering. Removing SPA also hurts performance, indicating that supervised generation alone is insufficient to optimize user-preferred slates.

Within SPA, removing the primary reward causes a larger degradation than removing the auxiliary reward, confirming that user feedback provides the dominant alignment signal while slate-level quality signals offer complementary guidance. The full model achieves the best performance by combining both signals with confidence-aware calibration. Finally, removing conservative regularization results in a significant decline, validating the importance of constraining policy deviation during preference alignment.

Table 5 further examines the supervision objectives in GL2P. Removing either ℒsideps\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{eps}}_{\mathrm{sid}} or ℒsidfb\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{fb}}_{\mathrm{sid}} reduces both metrics, indicating that exposure-order supervision provides structural guidance for slate generation, while feedback-aware supervision refines generation according to user responses. Only their joint supervision enables OGR to learn stable and effective slate-level sequential dependencies.

Efficiency Analysis

For a fair and comprehensive efficiency comparison, we consider two decoding modes for the generative baselines in Fig. 3. Beam-5 autoregressively generates a KK-item slate by serially decoding the DD-level SID of each slate position. Because all K×DK\times D SID tokens are generated one after another, completing the slate requires K​DKD consecutive autoregressive decoding steps, resulting in the sequential decoding depth DepthBeam​-​5=K​D\mathrm{Depth}_{\mathrm{Beam\text{-}5}}=KD. In contrast, Top-5 performs a single next-item beam search and directly returns the KK highest-scoring item candidates. The SID chains of all KK items are decoded in parallel within the same beam search, so the sequential decoding depth depends only on the DD intra-item decoding steps, giving DepthTop​-​5=D\mathrm{Depth}_{\mathrm{Top\text{-}5}}=D.

In OGR, the efficiency improvement arises from the reduction in sequential dependencies. Once the planned representation pmp_{m} is available, Decsid\mathrm{Dec}_{\mathrm{sid}} can generate its SID chain while Decplan\mathrm{Dec}_{\mathrm{plan}} continues producing subsequent preference representations. For position mm, the dd-th SID token smds_{m}^{d} becomes available after mm planning steps and dd intra-item SID-decoding steps, so its sequential dependency depth is m+dm+d. The complete slate is available when the final token sKDs_{K}^{D} is generated, giving DepthOGR=K+D\mathrm{Depth}_{\mathrm{OGR}}=K+D.

Accordingly, OGR reduces the sequential dependency depth from 𝒪⁡(K​D)\mathcal{O}(KD) to 𝒪⁡(K+D)\mathcal{O}(K+D) by overlapping each position’s SID decoding with preference planning for subsequent positions, while preserving cross-position dependencies through Decplan\mathrm{Dec}_{\mathrm{plan}}. Under our setting of K=5K=5 and D=4D=4, the idealized critical-path reduction factor is K​D/(K+D)=20/9≈2.22KD/(K+D)=20/9\approx 2.22. This shortened sequential path provides a structural explanation for the observed acceleration. As Fig. 3 shows, OGR achieves measured throughput improvements of 2.43×2.43\times and 2.49×2.49\times over TIGER-Beam and OneRec-Beam, respectively, while obtaining the highest NDCG@5. By contrast, the Top-5 variants require only one next-item beam search but achieve substantially lower recommendation quality because they return alternative next-item candidates without explicitly modeling dependencies and ordering preferences across slate positions. Consequently, these results suggest that OGR provides an effective quality–efficiency trade-off for generative slate recommendation.

Online A/B Testing

We conduct online A/B testing on Kuaishou with 3% of the production traffic. Compared with the existing system, OGR improves Effective Views, Comments, Likes, and Forwards by 1.120%, 2.954%, 0.505%, and 1.255%, respectively, demonstrating its effectiveness and practical value in real-world large-scale recommendation scenarios.

Conclusion

We propose OGR, an end-to-end generative framework for slate recommendation that realizes “Once Generated, Ranked.” OGR integrates TUSID for constructing recommendation-aware hierarchical SIDs and a list-wise generation architecture with preference alignment for directly producing ordered slates. Extensive offline experiments and online A/B testing demonstrate its effectiveness and practical impact in real-world recommendation scenarios.

Appendix B Appendix 1: Additional Related Work on SID Construction

The related work on SID construction methods is presented below:

Traditional recommender systems have long represented items using atomic IDs, a paradigm widely adopted in collaborative filtering and factorization methods (ItemKNN, MF, BPR-MF, and FISM) (Sarwar et al. 2001; Koren et al. 2009; Rendle et al. 2009; Kabbur et al. 2013), deep sequential models (GRU4Rec, Caser, NARM, and NextItNet) (Hidasi et al. 2016; Tang and Wang 2018a; Charikar et al. 2004; Yuan et al. 2019), and Transformer-based recommenders (SASRec, BERT4Rec, and S3-Rec) (Kang and McAuley 2018a; Sun et al. 2019; Zhou et al. 2020). However, atomic IDs are arbitrary and unstructured symbols that encode no shared item structure, hindering the effective modeling of sparsely observed, long-tail, and newly introduced items. To address this limitation, TIGER (Lin et al. 2025b) uses RQ-VAE to quantize content representations into hierarchical SIDs, while QARM and OneRec (Järvelin and Kekäläinen 2002; Deng et al. 2025; Zhou et al. 2025) adopt RQ-KMeans to improve codebook utilization and assignment balance. These studies establish the foundation for SIDs in generative recommendation, yet the effective integration of content semantics and local collaborative structures remains underexplored.

Existing semantic-collaborative SID construction methods broadly follow two directions. The first directly imposes collaborative constraints during quantization, as in LETTER, ETEGRec, HiGR, QuaSID, and AdaSID (Wang et al. 2024; Liu et al. 2025; Pang et al. 2026; Hu et al. 2026; Pan et al. 2026). However, jointly optimizing collaborative alignment with reconstruction and codebook objectives may introduce competing gradients, increasing the risk of training instability and codebook collapse. The second aligns semantic and behavioral representations in the continuous space before quantization, as in QARM, FORGE, OneSearch, SaviorRec, and GR4AD (Järvelin and Kekäläinen 2002; Fu et al. 2026; Chen et al. 2026; Yao et al. 2025; Xue et al. 2026). These approaches decouple representation learning from discrete encoding but typically rely on sampled item pairs and contrastive learning, making it difficult to fully capture local co-occurrence structures of varying strengths and limiting their suitability for generative slate recommendation.

Appendix C Appendix 2: B-Tags and C-Tags

In addition to Brand and Category, we use two multi-label high-level attributes for each item, as shown in Table 7. B-tags characterize the supply side of content, including how it is positioned, presented, and operated; C-tags characterize the demand side, including the user need, value, scenario, and target audience. The two tag records are separately converted into text and encoded by the shared text encoder to obtain eiBte_{i}^{\mathrm{Bt}} and eiCte_{i}^{\mathrm{Ct}}, which are fused with the multimodal item representation as described in the main text.

Appendix D Appendix 3: RQ-KMeans for SID Construction

Given the unified item representation eiunie_{i}^{\mathrm{uni}}, we apply residual-quantized K-means (RQ-KMeans) to construct the hierarchical SID 𝐬i\mathbf{s}_{i}. RQ-KMeans recursively quantizes the residual representation, so that early codewords typically capture larger-scale variation, whereas later codewords encode the remaining residual detail.

Let ζi(1)=eiuni\zeta_{i}^{(1)}=e_{i}^{\mathrm{uni}} be the initial residual of item ii. Here, i∈{1,…,Nitem}i\in\{1,\ldots,N_{\mathrm{item}}\}, DD is the SID depth used in the main paper, ndcbn_{d}^{\mathrm{cb}} is the codebook size at depth dd, and

Ξ(d)={ξn(d)}n=1ndcb\Xi^{(d)}=\{\xi_{n}^{(d)}\}_{n=1}^{n_{d}^{\mathrm{cb}}}

denotes the depth-dd codebook. RQ-KMeans assigns the residual to its nearest centroid:

sid=arg⁡minn∈{1,…,ndcb}⁡‖ζi(d)−ξn(d)‖22.s_{i}^{d}=\arg\min_{n\in\{1,\ldots,n_{d}^{\mathrm{cb}}\}}\left\lVert\zeta_{i}^{(d)}-\xi_{n}^{(d)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}. (19)

The residual is then updated as

ζi(d+1)=ζi(d)−ξsid(d).\zeta_{i}^{(d+1)}=\zeta_{i}^{(d)}-\xi_{s_{i}^{d}}^{(d)}. (20)

After DD quantization levels, the SID and reconstructed representation are

𝐬i=(si1,…,siD),e^irq=∑d=1Dξsid(d).\mathbf{s}_{i}=(s_{i}^{1},\ldots,s_{i}^{D}),\qquad\widehat{e}_{i}^{\mathrm{rq}}=\sum_{d=1}^{D}\xi_{s_{i}^{d}}^{(d)}. (21)

During validation, testing, and online inference, the codebooks are frozen and each item is encoded by recursively selecting the nearest centroid at every depth. This ensures a consistent SID vocabulary across training and evaluation.

Appendix E Appendix 4: Details of Collaborative Injection

Preliminaries of CountSketch

CountSketch was originally introduced for frequency estimation in data streams (Charikar et al. 2002). Given a frequency vector x∈ℝnvocabx\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\mathrm{vocab}}}, it maintains a compressed table 𝐆cs∈ℝnrow×nbucket\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{cs}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\mathrm{row}}\times n_{\mathrm{bucket}}}. For row vv, a bucket hash 𝔥v:[nvocab]→[nbucket]\mathfrak{h}_{v}:[n_{\mathrm{vocab}}]\rightarrow[n_{\mathrm{bucket}}] and a sign hash ςv:[nvocab]→{−1,+1}\varsigma_{v}:[n_{\mathrm{vocab}}]\rightarrow\{-1,+1\} map a weighted update (j,υ)(j,\upsilon) to

𝐆cs,v,𝔥v​(j)←𝐆cs,v,𝔥v​(j)+ςv(j)υ,v=1,…,nrow.\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{cs},v,\mathfrak{h}_{v}(j)}\leftarrow\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{cs},v,\mathfrak{h}_{v}(j)}+\varsigma_{v}(j)\upsilon,\qquad v=1,\ldots,n_{\mathrm{row}}. (22)

The corresponding row estimate is

x^j(v)=ςv​(j)​𝐆cs,v,𝔥v​(j).\widehat{x}_{j}^{(v)}=\varsigma_{v}(j)\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{cs},v,\mathfrak{h}_{v}(j)}. (23)

For independent sign hashes, cross terms caused by unrelated coordinates have zero expectation; additional buckets reduce collisions, while the median across independent rows makes classical point queries robust to an occasional large collision.

CCE uses only the two feature-mapping operations needed for collaborative representation learning: fixed-dimensional bucket hashing and random sign hashing. It shares one bucket hash and one sign hash across all center items and constructs an nbucketn_{\mathrm{bucket}}-dimensional sketch for each item. Unlike classical CountSketch, CCE does not recover individual coordinates or aggregate multiple point-query estimates. It directly applies a signed-log transform, normalization, and random projection to the shared-hash sketch. This design requires one bucket update per observed context pair and reduces the item–context storage to a fixed-dimensional representation per item.

CountSketch-Based Collaborative Embedding

Building on the bucket-hashing and sign-hashing operations summarized above, CCE uses signed hashing as a fixed-dimensional feature map for item-level collaborative structures.

Let ℛu+=(ȷu,1,…,ȷu,Lu+)\mathcal{R}_{u}^{+}=(\jmath_{u,1},\ldots,\jmath_{u,L_{u}^{+}}) denote the high-quality positive-feedback training prefix of user uu. Validation and test interactions are excluded from collaborative feature construction. For each item ii, we define its uncompressed local-context vector xi∈ℝnvocabx_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\mathrm{vocab}}} as

xi[j]=∑u∑p,q:ȷu,p=i,ȷu,q=j0<|p−q|≤ω1|p−q|,x_{i}[j]=\sum_{u}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p,q:\;\jmath_{u,p}=i,\;\jmath_{u,q}=j\\ 0<|p-q|\leq\omega\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{|p-q|}, (24)

where nvocabn_{\mathrm{vocab}} is the item vocabulary size and ω\omega is the context-window radius. The value xi​[j]x_{i}[j] measures the distance-weighted local co-occurrence between center item ii and contextual item jj, with nearby interactions receiving larger weights. When the same item appears at different sequence positions, j=ij=i is permitted; such repeated-item co-occurrences are retained, while only the identical position q=pq=p is excluded.

Explicitly storing all {xi}\{x_{i}\} requires an item–context matrix whose size grows with the item vocabulary. CCE instead employs one bucket hash

h:[nvocab]→[nbucket]h:[n_{\mathrm{vocab}}]\rightarrow[n_{\mathrm{bucket}}] (25)

and one sign hash

σ:[nvocab]→{−1,+1},\sigma:[n_{\mathrm{vocab}}]\rightarrow\{-1,+1\}, (26)

which are shared by all center items. The compressed collaborative sketch of item ii is defined as

𝒞i[ν]=∑j:h⁡(j)=νσ(j)xi[j],ν=1,…,nbucket.\mathcal{C}_{i}[\nu]=\sum_{j:h(j)=\nu}\sigma(j)x_{i}[j],\qquad\nu=1,\ldots,n_{\mathrm{bucket}}. (27)

Equivalently, when contextual item j=ȷu,qj=\jmath_{u,q} occurs within the local window of center item i=ȷu,pi=\jmath_{u,p}, the corresponding sketch is updated by

𝒞i​[h⁡(j)]←𝒞i​[h⁡(j)]+σ⁡(j)|p−q|.\mathcal{C}_{i}[h(j)]\leftarrow\mathcal{C}_{i}[h(j)]+\frac{\sigma(j)}{|p-q|}. (28)

Sharing hh and σ\sigma across all center items makes their compressed contextual distributions directly comparable. In particular, the raw sketches satisfy

𝔼⁡[⟨𝒞i,𝒞i′⟩]=⟨xi,xi′⟩.\mathbb{E}\left[\left\langle\mathcal{C}_{i},\mathcal{C}_{i^{\prime}}\right\rangle\right]=\left\langle x_{i},x_{i^{\prime}}\right\rangle. (29)

A contextual item jj shared by items ii and i′i^{\prime} contributes

σ​(j)2​xi​[j]​xi′​[j]=xi​[j]​xi′​[j],\sigma(j)^{2}x_{i}[j]x_{i^{\prime}}[j]=x_{i}[j]x_{i^{\prime}}[j], (30)

whereas a cross term produced by unrelated items j≠j′j\neq j^{\prime} contains σ⁡(j)​σ​(j′)\sigma(j)\sigma(j^{\prime}) and has zero expectation. Therefore, common local contexts make consistent positive contributions, while unrelated hash collisions do not systematically increase the raw-sketch similarity.

The sketch buckets may still contain large values caused by highly frequent co-occurrences. We therefore apply a signed-log transformation:

zi​[ν]=sign⁡(𝒞i​[ν])​log⁡(1+|𝒞i​[ν]|).z_{i}[\nu]=\operatorname{sign}\left(\mathcal{C}_{i}[\nu]\right)\log\left(1+\left|\mathcal{C}_{i}[\nu]\right|\right). (31)

This transformation preserves the sign of each aggregated bucket while compressing its magnitude, thereby reducing the dominance of frequent contextual items and large residual bucket values.

We then perform per-item ℓ2\ell_{2} normalization:

z¯i=zimax⁡(∥zi∥2,ϑn),\bar{z}_{i}=\frac{z_{i}}{\max\left(\lVert z_{i}\rVert_{2},\vartheta_{\mathrm{n}}\right)}, (32)

where ϑn>0\vartheta_{\mathrm{n}}>0 is a numerical stability constant. A shared fixed random projection maps the normalized sketch to the collaborative embedding space:

e~icol=Λcol​z¯i,Λcol∈ℝncol×nbucket,\widetilde{e}_{i}^{\mathrm{col}}=\Lambda_{\mathrm{col}}\bar{z}_{i},\qquad\Lambda_{\mathrm{col}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\mathrm{col}}\times n_{\mathrm{bucket}}}, (33)

where ncoln_{\mathrm{col}} matches the semantic embedding dimension. The projected representation is further normalized as

eicol=e~icolmax⁡(‖e~icol‖2,ϑn).e_{i}^{\mathrm{col}}=\frac{\widetilde{e}_{i}^{\mathrm{col}}}{\max\left(\left\lVert\widetilde{e}_{i}^{\mathrm{col}}\right\rVert_{2},\vartheta_{\mathrm{n}}\right)}. (34)

Confidence-Aware Weighting

For each user uu, let ℛu+=(ȷu,1,…,ȷu,Lu+)\mathcal{R}_{u}^{+}=(\jmath_{u,1},\ldots,\jmath_{u,L_{u}^{+}}) denote the chronologically ordered high-quality positive-feedback training sequence, where ȷu,p\jmath_{u,p} is the item at position pp and Lu+L_{u}^{+} is the sequence length. Validation and test interactions are excluded from ℛu+\mathcal{R}_{u}^{+}.

Given the context-window radius ω\omega, user uu contributes contextual information to item ii if ii occurs at some position pp in ℛu+\mathcal{R}_{u}^{+} and there exists another position qq within its context window. We define the distinct-user support of item ii as

Ui=∑u𝟏[∃p,q∈{1,…,Lu+}:ȷu,p=i,0<|p−q|≤ω],U_{i}=\sum_{u}\mathbf{1}\left[\begin{gathered}\exists\,p,q\in\{1,\ldots,L_{u}^{+}\}:\\ \jmath_{u,p}=i,\qquad 0<|p-q|\leq\omega\end{gathered}\right], (35)

where 𝟏​[⋅]\mathbf{1}[\cdot] is an indicator function. For a given user uu, the indicator equals 11 if the user’s sequence provides at least one valid contextual update for item ii, and equals 00 otherwise. Since each user corresponds to only one binary indicator, repeated occurrences of item ii or multiple contextual updates from the same user do not increase UiU_{i}. Therefore, UiU_{i} counts the number of distinct users that contribute collaborative evidence to item ii, rather than the total number of interactions.

Since distinct-user support is typically long-tailed, we first apply logarithmic compression and then convert it into an item-level collaborative confidence:

γi=log⁡(1+Ui)log⁡(1+Ui)+τ,αi=αcol​γi,\gamma_{i}=\frac{\log(1+U_{i})}{\log(1+U_{i})+\tau},\qquad\alpha_{i}=\alpha_{\mathrm{col}}\gamma_{i}, (36)

where τ>0\tau>0 controls the saturation speed of the confidence and αcol∈[0,1]\alpha_{\mathrm{col}}\in[0,1] specifies the maximum collaborative weight. The logarithmic transformation compresses large differences among high-support items and introduces diminishing returns as additional users are observed. Consequently, items with sufficient behavioral support can make greater use of collaborative information without allowing highly popular items to dominate solely because of their interaction scale.

A smaller UiU_{i} produces a smaller αi\alpha_{i}, downweighting potentially unreliable collaborative evidence for interaction-sparse or cold-start items. In particular, Ui=0U_{i}=0 directly gives γi=αi=0\gamma_{i}=\alpha_{i}=0, so an item without valid collaborative support relies entirely on its semantic representation.

Before fusion, the semantic representation is normalized as

e¯isem=eisemmax⁡(∥eisem∥2,ϑn).\bar{e}_{i}^{\mathrm{sem}}=\frac{e_{i}^{\mathrm{sem}}}{\max\left(\lVert e_{i}^{\mathrm{sem}}\rVert_{2},\vartheta_{\mathrm{n}}\right)}. (37)

The unified representation is then constructed through confidence-weighted concatenation:

eiuni=[1−αi​e¯isem;αi​eicol].e_{i}^{\mathrm{uni}}=\left[\sqrt{1-\alpha_{i}}\,\bar{e}_{i}^{\mathrm{sem}};\sqrt{\alpha_{i}}\,e_{i}^{\mathrm{col}}\right]. (38)

This concatenation retains the complementary structures of the semantic and collaborative branches, while αi\alpha_{i} controls their relative contributions according to item-level behavioral support.

When both branches are nonzero and unit-normalized, the square-root coefficients preserve the norm of the unified representation:

‖eiuni‖22\displaystyle\left\lVert e_{i}^{\mathrm{uni}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2} =(1−αi)​‖e¯isem‖22+αi​‖eicol‖22\displaystyle=(1-\alpha_{i})\left\lVert\bar{e}_{i}^{\mathrm{sem}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\alpha_{i}\left\lVert e_{i}^{\mathrm{col}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2} (39)
=(1−αi)+αi\displaystyle=(1-\alpha_{i})+\alpha_{i}
=1.\displaystyle=1.

Thus, under the stated nonzero, unit-normalized condition, CAW adjusts the relative contribution of semantic and collaborative information without introducing item-dependent variation in the overall representation scale.

The complete construction of the collaborative embeddings and their confidence-aware fusion with the semantic representations is summarized in Algorithm 1.

Appendix F Appendix 5: Details of Reward-Consistent Calibration

Due to confidentiality constraints, the full industrial reward schema cannot be disclosed. We therefore report the retained feedback signals, fixed weights, and exposure-only calibration procedure used in the experiments.

For user uu, let ℰu\mathcal{E}_{u} be the collection of complete slates recorded in the training exposure log. Operationally, the “candidate rollouts” in the main paper refer to evaluating logged candidate slates under the policy, rather than generating new slates for reward assignment. The alignment action set 𝒜u⊆ℰu\mathcal{A}_{u}\subseteq\mathcal{E}_{u} is therefore formed only from these logged exposure slates. For each a∈𝒜ua\in\mathcal{A}_{u}, the frozen reference policy and the current policy are used only to compute the corresponding slate log-likelihoods ℓ0​(a∣u)\ell_{0}(a\mid u) and ℓθ​(a∣u)\ell_{\theta}(a\mid u). Newly generated or counterfactual slates are not assigned observed-feedback rewards and are excluded from reward calibration.

Primary Reward

For an exposed item at position kk of action aa, let bu,a,kevb_{u,a,k}^{\mathrm{ev}}, bu,a,kcompb_{u,a,k}^{\mathrm{comp}}, bu,a,klikeb_{u,a,k}^{\mathrm{like}}, bu,a,kshareb_{u,a,k}^{\mathrm{share}}, bu,a,kskipb_{u,a,k}^{\mathrm{skip}}, and bu,a,kdislikeb_{u,a,k}^{\mathrm{dislike}} be binary indicators for an effective view, completion, like, share, immediate skip, and dislike, respectively. A zero means that the item was exposed but the event did not occur. We use the following fixed slate reward:

ru,apri=1K​∑k=1K(CLOSE\displaystyle r_{u,a}^{\mathrm{pri}}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\Bigl( 0.10​bu,a,kev+0.15​bu,a,kcomp\displaystyle 0.10\,b_{u,a,k}^{\mathrm{ev}}+0.15\,b_{u,a,k}^{\mathrm{comp}} (40)
+0.20​bu,a,klike+0.15​bu,a,kshare\displaystyle+0.20\,b_{u,a,k}^{\mathrm{like}}+0.15\,b_{u,a,k}^{\mathrm{share}}
OPEN−0.15​bu,a,kskip−0.25​bu,a,kdislike).\displaystyle-0.15\,b_{u,a,k}^{\mathrm{skip}}-0.25\,b_{u,a,k}^{\mathrm{dislike}}\Bigr).

The six signals cover consumption quality, explicit positive actions, and explicit negative actions. Effective view receives the smallest positive weight; completion and share receive equal intermediate weights; and like receives the largest positive weight. Dislike incurs a larger penalty than immediate skip. The absolute weights sum to one, which keeps the per-position scale easy to interpret.

Auxiliary Reward

We retain only intra-slate diversity and novelty. Let e¯i\bar{e}_{i} be the unit-normalized semantic representation of item ii, let cic_{i} be its exposure count in the training split, and define the Laplace-smoothed total C=∑j∈ℐ(cj+1)C=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}}(c_{j}+1). For the exposed item sequence (yu,a,1,…,yu,a,K)(y_{u,a,1},\ldots,y_{u,a,K}), the two scores are

du,a\displaystyle d_{u,a} =2K⁡(K−1)​∑1≤p<q≤K1−e¯yu,a,p⊤​e¯yu,a,q2,\displaystyle=\frac{2}{K(K-1)}\sum_{1\leq p<q\leq K}\frac{1-\bar{e}_{y_{u,a,p}}^{\top}\bar{e}_{y_{u,a,q}}}{2}, (41)
nu,a\displaystyle n_{u,a} =1K​∑k=1K−log⁡((cyu,a,k+1)/C)log⁡C.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{-\log\!\left((c_{y_{u,a,k}}+1)/C\right)}{\log C}.

Both terms lie in [0,1][0,1]: du,ad_{u,a} is the mean pairwise cosine distance, and nu,an_{u,a} is larger for less frequently exposed items. The auxiliary reward is

ru,aaux=0.90​du,a+0.10​nu,a.r_{u,a}^{\mathrm{aux}}=0.90\,d_{u,a}+0.10\,n_{u,a}. (42)

These fixed weights are used throughout the alignment experiments. Diversity receives the dominant weight because it directly measures redundancy at the slate level; novelty is retained as a smaller secondary correction.

Relative Reward

For o∈{pri,aux}o\in\{\mathrm{pri},\mathrm{aux}\}, we compute statistics over the same exposure-only action set:

Meanuo\displaystyle\operatorname{Mean}_{u}^{o} =1|𝒜u|​∑a∈𝒜uru,ao,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}_{u}|}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{u}}r_{u,a}^{o}, (43)
(Stduo)2\displaystyle\left(\operatorname{Std}_{u}^{o}\right)^{2} =1|𝒜u|​∑a∈𝒜u(ru,ao−Meanuo)2.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}_{u}|}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{u}}\left(r_{u,a}^{o}-\operatorname{Mean}_{u}^{o}\right)^{2}.

The relative reward score used in the main paper is

δu,ao=ru,ao−Meanuomax⁡(Stduo,ε).\delta_{u,a}^{o}=\frac{r_{u,a}^{o}-\operatorname{Mean}_{u}^{o}}{\max(\operatorname{Std}_{u}^{o},\varepsilon)}. (44)

A positive δu,ao\delta_{u,a}^{o} indicates that the slate performs better than the user’s candidate average, while a negative value indicates worse relative performance. Users with fewer than two logged slates are excluded from the alignment batch. If a reward component is constant within 𝒜u\mathcal{A}_{u}, its standardized score is zero for every action and it contributes no preference direction.
